title: The first screen of an inventory tool
metaTitle: The first screen of an inventory tool
excerpt: The first screen of an inventory tool is for the person on the floor. Show the next item in their hand and one action. A dashboard built for the office makes them work around it.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky, a single subject you can name without a legend.
caption: One subject, easy to name. The first screen on the floor should be that plain. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an inventory tool show the floor first?
faqs.answer: Show the next useful object and one action, usually the item in their hand, the bin they are standing at, or the next line on the count. The action is confirm, scan, or mark short. A chart for the office can live somewhere else, and it should not be the screen they land on with a box under one arm.

faqs.question: Why is a dashboard the wrong first screen?
faqs.answer: A dashboard answers the office question: how is the warehouse doing. The floor question is: what do I do with this item. Charts, tours, and module menus delay that answer. People on the floor will work around a dashboard with paper, and the paper becomes the inventory that is actually true.

faqs.question: How should the screen behave with one hand?
faqs.answer: The current item should be readable at arm's length, in large type, with the name that is printed on the box. The action sits where a thumb can reach without shifting the grip. Scanning can be the primary action. Typing a code is the fallback, not the assumed path.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Inventory tool UX on the first screen belongs to the person on the floor, not the person in the office. Show the next useful object and one action. Name the object. Name the action. A tour, or a dashboard of the whole warehouse, makes them put the scanner down.

The object is the item in their hand, the bin in front of them, or the next line of the count they already started. The action is confirm the quantity, scan the code, or mark the line short. If the screen opens on a chart, they will finish the count on paper. The paper will be right. The tool will be a rumor.

## Two people, two first screens

The office wants a picture of stock, value, and exceptions. That is a real job, and it can have a screen. It is not the screen that should open when someone clocks onto a count, a pick, or a receipt on the floor.

The floor is interrupted. They have one hand. The light is bad. The wifi drops between aisles. Gloves make small targets annoying. The first view has to be readable at arm's length and tappable without a precise tap. A dense table that looks impressive in a desktop review fails in the aisle in under a minute.

Jakob Nielsen wrote that people often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is obvious. On the floor the clock is harsher, because they are holding a box. The value is the next line, named the way the box is named. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the polite version of a picker who locks the phone and goes back to a printed list.

If you only have budget for one excellent screen, build the floor's. The office can survive a plainer report. The floor cannot survive a report dressed up as their work.

## Name the object the way the box does

Use the name printed on the carton, the bin code painted on the rack, and the quantity they are checking. Internal titles, supplier codes they never see, and a stock keeping unit with no words are office objects. Show the human name first. Put the code second, large enough to check against the label.

If they scanned in, the scanned object is the whole screen. Photo if you have a true photo of the product, the name, the expected quantity, and one control to confirm or change it. Do not show a feed of other modules. Do not show a celebration. Confirm is the celebration.

If they did not scan, the object is the next line of the task they were given. Pick list, cycle count, or receipt. Show one line at a time if the environment is rough. A list of fifty lines is the second view, for when they need to jump. The first view is the line you think they should do next, and a way to say "not this one."

Empty work is an object too. "No counts assigned in this zone" is useful. A zeroed chart is not. Tell them whether to switch zone or wait. Switching zone is an action. Waiting is a sentence. Do not leave a blank table and call it done.

One noun from the label to the button. If the rack says Bin C4, the screen says Bin C4. If the button says Confirm 12, the success says 12 confirmed for that bin. "Submit transaction" is how the office talks. The floor will not adopt your noun if the paint on the rack already chose one.

## One action, sized for the aisle

The action is large. It sits at the bottom of the phone, where the thumb already is. Confirm. Or Scan next. Or Mark short. One of those, visually primary. The others can exist as text buttons if they are real alternatives, not as a toolbar of six equal icons.

Scan can be the primary action when the task is identification. Open the camera or the sled scanner without a tour step. If the scan misses, the fallback is type the code, on the same screen, with the last camera frame or the expected item still visible. Do not dump them into a different mode called "manual entry" with no way back.

Do not ask them to choose a warehouse, a reason code, and a cost center before the first confirm. Defaults from the shift start can cover warehouse and zone. Rare reason codes belong behind Mark short, not in front of every happy scan. The office loves reason codes. The floor loves finishing the aisle. Collect the code only when the line is an exception.

Quantity changes should be deliberate and hard to do by accident, without being hard to do on purpose. A stepper with a large hit area beats a tiny keyboard for a one-unit correction. Typing remains available for a real recount. Do not make them type 12 when they meant to accept 12. Accept is the default action when the expected quantity is on screen.

Sign-in should happen at the start of the shift, not between every bin. A session that expires in the middle of a count, and returns them to a marketing login with no draft, will train them to avoid the tool. Keep the count on the device until it is synced, and say that it is stored on the device.

## What a tour and a dashboard steal

A tour that points at the menu, the search icon, and the avatar spends the time they are holding the box. Skip it. The first successful scan teaches the product. A sentence on the empty state teaches the rest: "Scan the bin, then the item."

A dashboard as the home screen answers a question they did not ask. Units on hand. Shrink this month. Top movers. Those numbers are for someone at a desk who can act on them. On a phone in an aisle they are a delay and a mis-tap surface. If the floor must see one office number, make it the exception that changes their next scan, such as a hold on that bin. Put it on the line, not in a chart.

Module grids are the same mistake in icon form. Receive, Count, Transfer, Adjust, Reports. The person opened the app from a task. Land in that task. If they have two tasks, the first screen is the list of those two tasks, with the names the supervisor used. It is not a catalog of your capabilities.

Motion, sound, and haptics can confirm a scan. Keep them short. A full-screen animation between items is a tax per bin. People who prefer reduced motion, and people who are simply in a loud aisle, should get a visible confirmation that does not depend on the sound. A check on the line is enough.

## What to leave off this screen

Leave valuation off. Leave supplier portals, purchase orders, and user admin off. Leave the company story off. The floor does not need the brand film to count a bin.

Leave social proof and "tips." A tip that covers the quantity is an obstacle. If a tip is essential, such as "count sealed cases as 12," put it in one line under the item name, every time, not as a dismissible card they must swipe while holding a knife or a clipboard.

Leave multi-select and batch edit off the first view. Those are office gestures. On the floor they cause accidental confirms of the wrong lines. One line, one action, then the next line.

If the office insists the first screen prove the product is "serious," show a serious line: the right bin, the right name, the right quantity, the right action. Seriousness is accuracy they can feel in the first minute. A chart is a costume.


Watch a count with the scanner sled if that is the hardware the floor actually uses. A screen designed for a bare thumb on glass can hide the action behind the sled's grip. The primary button has to clear the hardware, not only the mockup in the design file. If the sled covers the bottom edge, move Confirm into the thumb zone that remains, and test it with the case on. The case is part of the device. The conference-room phone without a case is not the product you are shipping to the aisle.
## Review it in the aisle, not in the conference room

Walk the first screen with someone who does the count, on the device they actually use, under the lights you actually have. You are listening for the name they say when they look at the box, and whether that name is the largest text on the screen.

Time the path from unlock to a confirmed line. It should not include a tour, a dashboard, or a warehouse picker if they already chose a zone at shift start. If it includes those, move them out of the way and watch again.

Then break it. Scan the wrong bin. Lose the network. Those frames are part of the same job, and the next piece is [errors in an inventory tool](/blog/errors-in-an-inventory-tool). A first screen that only works on the office wifi, with the founder's hands free, is a demo.

If you want that floor screen designed as the product, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). The office report can follow. The aisle will not wait for it.
